justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with only modest drift upward over time. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to what would have been the prevailing price level, assuming no major overnight catalysts and typical mean-reversion tendencies in liquid markets. The one-week estimate nudged slightly higher to reflect a mild positive drift assumption, consistent with long-run equity risk premium expectations scaled down to a weekly horizon. The one-month estimate continued that gradual upward bias, though the increment remains small because short-term momentum and macro conditions were not strongly directional at the time of the forecast.

The confidence interval widths expand predictably as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty that characterizes random walk models. At one day, realized volatility in the underlying asset likely runs somewhere in the range of 1–2%, so a roughly plus-or-minus 5 points around 209.5 captures the bulk of expected daily moves. By one week, the interval widens to roughly plus-or-minus 11 points, and by one month it reaches roughly plus-or-minus 22 points, consistent with annualized volatility in the mid-teens percentage range. I also factored in some additional uncertainty at longer horizons due to the possibility of regime shifts that pure historical volatility models tend to understate.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharper-than-expected jobs report, renewed inflation fears prompting aggressive Federal Reserve rhetoric, or a credit event in a systemically important institution — could easily breach the lower bound of the one-month interval. Geopolitical shocks or liquidity crises tend to produce fat-tailed outcomes that normal distribution assumptions underweight.

On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, a dovish pivot signal from central banks, or a resolution of ongoing geopolitical tensions could push prices well above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is more time for positive catalysts to compound. My intervals are calibrated at 90%, meaning I explicitly acknowledged a 10% combined probability of outcomes outside the stated range, but in practice tail events in financial markets occur more frequently than that, so these bounds should be treated as reasonable guides rather than hard limits.
